explanations.explanation: Close, baker, but this one is flipped. Moses tells Israel the LORD said to him, “You shall not cross the Jordan.” So he isn't the one leading them over. The LORD Himself goes across ahead of the people, and Joshua goes across ahead of them too.

You've got it, baker. Moses says the LORD told him, “You shall not cross the Jordan.” He's a hundred and twenty and no longer able to come and go. I think that's a tough thing to say out loud to a whole nation.

Joshua it is. Moses says, “Joshua will cross ahead of you, as the LORD has said.” Joshua is the man Moses is about to call up in front of everybody. The LORD goes first, and Joshua goes ahead of the people.

Good guess, friend. Caleb is the man the LORD calls “My servant Caleb” (Numbers 14:24). But Caleb isn't the name Moses gives here. Moses says Joshua will cross ahead of the people, as the LORD has said.

Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), so I see why he came to mind. But Aaron had already died on the mountaintop (Numbers 20:28). The man Moses names here is Joshua, who will cross ahead of the people.
Not quite. Moses says the LORD will deliver those nations over to Israel. Then he adds, “…you must do to them exactly as I have commanded you.” Exactly means exactly, with no freestyle.

That's right. Moses says the LORD will deliver them over, and then Israel must do to them “…exactly as I have commanded you.” There's no room for doing it their own way. It's like a recipe card, friend. You follow it, you don't remix it.

explanations.answer: The LORD their God goes with them
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses says, “…it is the LORD your God who goes with you; He will never leave you nor forsake you.” That's the whole reason he gives. Their courage isn't resting on their own strength.

explanations.answer: Joshua has never lost a battle
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a nice reason, but Moses never says it. He doesn't point to Joshua's record at all. He says, “…it is the LORD your God who goes with you…”

explanations.answer: The nations are already running away
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't say that, friend. Nothing in his words has those nations on the run. His reason is that the LORD their God goes with them, and “He will never leave you nor forsake you.”

Inheritance is right. Moses says the land is the one the LORD swore to their fathers, and Joshua will give it to the people as an inheritance. That's something handed down, and here it rests on what the LORD swore. Joshua's job is to go with the people and give it to them, and the LORD Himself goes before him (Deuteronomy 31:8).

I see the pull, since Moses has been talking about nations being destroyed. But that's not the word. He says Joshua will give the land to them as an inheritance, which is a gift the LORD swore to their fathers.

A fortress sounds sturdy, but it isn't what Moses says. He tells Joshua the land is the one the LORD swore to their fathers, and he'll give it to the people as an inheritance. That word is about what's handed down.

explanations.answer: The priests and the elders of Israel
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Moses gave the law to “…the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and to all the elders of Israel.” That's two groups holding it, not just one person. Me, I'd be nervous with only one keeper, because my hands are a mustache and I once dropped a whole tray of dough with them.

I get why Joshua came to mind, since he's the new leader. But this verse doesn't mention him or any commanders. Moses hands the law to the priests, the sons of Levi who carried the ark, and to all the elders of Israel.
Judges aren't named in this verse, friend. Moses gives the written law to the priests who carried the ark of the covenant and to all the elders of Israel. That's the whole list.
Yes. Moses says, “…you are to read this law in the hearing of all Israel.” Every seven years, the whole gathering hears it. That's a lot of folks, so I hope somebody warmed up their voice.

explanations.answer: Count the people tribe by tribe
explanations.explanation: No counting here, baker. Moses never mentions a headcount at this gathering. What he says is, “…you are to read this law in the hearing of all Israel.”

explanations.answer: Choose a new leader for Israel
explanations.explanation: Not at this gathering. Moses says the job is to “…read this law in the hearing of all Israel.” Picking a leader isn't part of what he describes here.
That's it. Moses says to assemble “…men, women, children, and the foreigners within your gates…” The reading isn't just for the folks born in the camp. Everybody gets a seat.
Edom isn't mentioned here. Moses talks about the foreigners within their gates, meaning the ones living among them. The people he names are men, women, children, and those foreigners.

Egypt's officials aren't on the guest list, friend. Moses says to gather “…men, women, children, and the foreigners within your gates…” It's about people already living among them, not visiting officials.
Follow is the word. Moses wants them to listen and learn “…to fear the LORD your God and to follow carefully all the words of this law.” Hearing it is only step one. Following it is where it lands.

I know some folks love a good debate, but that's not what Moses says. He wants them to listen and learn and then follow carefully all the words of this law. It's a hearing-and-doing plan, not a panel discussion.
Moses doesn't tell them to change the law, baker. He says to listen and learn to fear the LORD your God and to follow carefully all the words of this law. Following means keeping it as it was given.

That's right. Moses says their children who don't know the law will listen and learn to fear the LORD your God, “…as long as you live in the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess.” The reading in verse 12 gathers everyone: men, women, children, and the foreigners within your gates. So the children aren't left out of the room. They're right there in the crowd, listening.

Not this time. Moses says the children who don't know the law will listen and learn to fear the LORD your God. And it lasts “…as long as you live in the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess.”

Commission is right. The LORD says, “Call Joshua and present yourselves at the Tent of Meeting, so that I may commission him.” Moses isn't doing the commissioning here. The LORD is, and Moses walks Joshua there.
The LORD does have some heavy words coming for Moses, but that's not why He calls Joshua to the tent. He says it's “…so that I may commission him.” Commission is the word on the table.
I see why that might sound likely, but the LORD never says test. He says, “Call Joshua and present yourselves at the Tent of Meeting, so that I may commission him.” It's an appointment, not an exam.

explanations.answer: Turn to foreign gods and break His covenant
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says they “…will rise up and prostitute themselves with the foreign gods of the land they are entering.” Then He says, “They will forsake Me and break the covenant I have made with them.” This is a hard word to hear.

explanations.answer: Stay faithful to Him for good
explanations.explanation: I wish that were the line, friend. But the LORD says the opposite. He says they “…will forsake Me and break the covenant I have made with them.”

explanations.answer: Refuse to go in and turn back
explanations.explanation: That's not what the LORD says here. He says they will go into the land. Once they're there, they “…will rise up and prostitute themselves with the foreign gods of the land they are entering.”

explanations.answer: If it's because their God isn't with them
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says they will say, “Have not these disasters come upon us because our God is no longer with us?” It's a question they ask when the troubles pile up. I think that one carries a lot of ache.

explanations.answer: Why Moses ever left them behind
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't mention Moses in what the people will ask. He says they'll say, “Have not these disasters come upon us because our God is no longer with us?” Their question is about God being no longer with them.

explanations.answer: If Joshua led them the wrong way
explanations.explanation: Joshua isn't in that question, baker. The LORD says the people will ask, “Have not these disasters come upon us because our God is no longer with us?” Notice where they point. It's not at a leader or a route, but at God being no longer with them. I think that's a heavy question to hear ahead of time.
That's right. The LORD says, “…on that day I will surely hide My face because of all the evil they have done by turning to other gods.” He names the reason Himself. It's a serious line.
Not this time. The LORD says He will surely hide His face “…because of all the evil they have done by turning to other gods.” The reason is right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: To be a witness for Him against them
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD has Moses write the song down and teach it to the Israelites so it stands as a witness for Him against them. Then He says it “…will not be forgotten from the lips of their descendants.” So this song is meant to be sung, and sung for a long time.

Nice thought, friend, but this song isn't a victory song. The LORD has Moses write it down and teach it to the Israelites so it stands as a witness for Him against them. He also says it “…will not be forgotten from the lips of their descendants.” Crossing the Jordan isn't what it's for.

explanations.answer: To honor Moses after he dies
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The LORD doesn't say the song honors Moses. He says to write it down and teach it “…so that it may be a witness for Me against them.”
Close, but the LORD says the opposite. He says the song “…will not be forgotten from the lips of their descendants.” It stays with the next generations, not just one.

That's right. The LORD says this song “…will not be forgotten from the lips of their descendants.” So it doesn't fade after one generation. It's meant to be handed down the line. Moses wrote it down and taught it to the Israelites that very day (Deuteronomy 31:22).

explanations.answer: He knows it before they enter the land
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, “…I know their inclination, even before I bring them into the land that I swore to give them.” He isn't waiting to find out. He already knows.

explanations.answer: He'll learn it once they settle in
explanations.explanation: That gets it backward, baker. The LORD says, “…I know their inclination, even before I bring them into the land…” He knows it ahead of time, not after they've unpacked.

explanations.answer: He'll see it after Moses dies
explanations.explanation: That's not how the LORD puts it. He says He knows their inclination “…even before I bring them into the land that I swore to give them.” The knowing comes before they ever cross over.

That's right. The LORD says to Joshua, “Be strong and courageous, for you will bring the Israelites into the land that I swore to give them, and I will be with you.” It's the same call Moses gave him. This time it comes straight from the LORD, with a promise attached.
Actually, He does. The LORD commissions Joshua with “Be strong and courageous…” the same words Moses used earlier. Then He adds, “…I will be with you.”

explanations.answer: Beside the ark of the covenant
explanations.explanation: Yes. Moses says, “Take this Book of the Law and place it beside the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God…” It stays there “…as a witness against you.” The Levites who carry the ark are the ones he tells.

explanations.answer: At the gate of the camp
explanations.explanation: A gate isn't mentioned here, friend. Moses tells the Levites to place the Book of the Law “…beside the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God…” That's where it stays.

Mount Ebal is a fine mountain, but it doesn't come up in these verses. Moses is talking to the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant. He tells them to place the book “…beside the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, so that it may remain there as a witness against you.” So the book's spot is right next to the ark.
I wish, baker, but Moses says the opposite. He says, “If you are already rebelling against the LORD while I am still alive, how much more will you rebel after my death!” More rebellion, not less.
You've got it. Moses says, “If you are already rebelling against the LORD while I am still alive, how much more will you rebel after my death!” That's his honest warning. It's a heavy one.

explanations.answer: The elders and officers of the tribes
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses says, “Assemble before me all the elders of your tribes and all your officers…” He wants them in front of him so he can speak these words in their hearing and call heaven and earth to witness against them. So the room he asks for is Israel's own leaders, tribe by tribe. These are heavy words, and he wants those leaders there to hear them.

explanations.answer: The kings of the nearby nations
explanations.explanation: Kings of other nations aren't on the list, friend. Moses asks for “…all the elders of your tribes and all your officers…” Those are Israel's own leaders.
Not those folks, baker. Moses asks for “…all the elders of your tribes and all your officers…” He wants Israel's leaders gathered before him to hear his words.

Yes. Moses says, “…after my death you will become utterly corrupt and turn from the path I have commanded you.” The path is the one he gave them. I think those are heavy words to say to people he has led. He adds that in the days to come, disaster will befall them because they will do evil in the sight of the LORD.
The land isn't what they turn from, friend. Moses says they will “…turn from the path I have commanded you.” He's talking about the way he told them to walk.
Moses doesn't mention leaders Joshua picks. He says, “…you will become utterly corrupt and turn from the path I have commanded you.” The path he gave is what they leave behind.

Disaster is the word. Moses says, “…in the days to come, disaster will befall you because you will do evil in the sight of the LORD…” It's a heavy ending to this stretch of his speech, so I'll just say it plainly.
I'd love that one, baker, but it isn't what Moses says. He says disaster will befall them because they'll do evil in the sight of the LORD. Peace is not on his list here.

Plenty sounds nice, friend, but Moses says something else. He says, “…in the days to come, disaster will befall you because you will do evil in the sight of the LORD…” Plenty doesn't follow evil in his words.
